Frequently Asked Questions
Any Questions?
When will my Wildgrain Box arrive?
We’ll ship your Wildgrain box within 1 business day. Delivery usually takes 1–2 business days (a day longer in remote areas). You’ll get an email with tracking once your box ships, plus email and SMS alerts when it’s out for delivery.
Can I adjust my deliveries?
Yes! You change your delivery frequency, skip, or cancel your membership at any time. For example, if you want to get your Wildgrain Box every 2 months instead of monthly, you can do that. You can make these adjustments on your Wildgrain account or by emailing us at hey@wildgrain.com .
Why is Wildgrain healthier?
We know that “healthy” is not typically the word that comes to mind when talking about carbs. But at Wildgrain, we approach making food differently.
All of our food is made with clean ingredients that are easy to understand and contain no preservatives. Beyond being clean replacements for your favorite grain carbs, our sourdough bread provides many health benefits. Our fermentation process digests the majority of the gluten; for this reason, some people with gluten sensitivities find that they can digest and enjoy sourdough bread. Sourdough bread also contains lactic acid, which helps your body absorb more nutrients (e.g. calcium, magnesium, and iron) than your body would from non-sourdough bread. Lastly, it contains prebiotics, which keep your gut biome healthy and also increase the bioavailability of nutrients.
Why is Wildgrain a membership?
Wildgrain sourdough breads take 26 hours to make, compared to 20 minutes for a supermarket loaf. It is difficult for an artisan-driven company like ours to source high-quality ingredients, staff our bakeries, and hand-shape each loaf without knowing roughly how many members we need to deliver to each month.
By becoming a member, you’re eating healthier products, supporting a small business and helping reduce food waste.

Q&A with Ismail Salhi and Johanna Hartzheim, Co-Founders of Wildgrain
January 21, 2025
Johanna Hartzheim and Ismail Salhi
Ismail Salhi , CEO and Co-Founder, and Johanna Hartzheim , Head of Product and Co-Founder, created Wildgrain out of a shared passion for making high-quality, artisanal bread more accessible to everyone across the U.S. Engineer, entrepreneur, and father, Ismail balances his roles as a business leader and technologist. After graduating from a prestigious Industrial Design school in Paris, Johanna joined forces with Ismail on a music industry project, leading to the creation of their first company, backed by Bose. The professional partnership blossomed into a personal one, and soon they moved to Boston. Expecting their first child and missing the quality bread and pastries from Paris, Johanna delved into Sourdough and French baking. Her culinary passion combined with Ismail’s interest in combining tech and tradition to promote artisanal baking techniques in an industry that often overlooks the importance of quality and craftsmanship, sparked the creation of Wildgrain, where she initially crafted all the breads and pastries by hand. Today, Wildgrain has grown into a thriving network of bakeries and pasta makers that has delivered over 8 million baked goods nationwide.
Tell us a little bit about your background and what led you to founding Wildgrain?
Our journey to Wildgrain started with a pivot from a previous venture in the tech and consumer hardware space when we were reassessing where we could make a meaningful impact. Our inspiration came from our own experiences— specifically, the loss of the amazing bread and pastries we were used to in Europe after moving to the U.S. We really missed the quality of the sourdoughs and other European breads. A trip to Germany reignited that passion when Johanna tasted sourdough at a friend’s house and thought, “this is the best bread I’ve ever had.” That led to an obsession with baking, and it wasn’t long before we decided to bring European-quality bread to American homes. Wildgrain was born out of that mission—to reimagine how people could enjoy artisanal baked goods at home. – Ismail
What is Wildgrain and why is it such a revolutionary product in the baked goods category?
Wildgrain isn’t just a subscription box—it’s an entirely new way to experience artisanal bread, pasta, cookies, and pastries. What makes us revolutionary is that we’re bringing European-quality, frozen baked goods directly to your door.This means no preservatives or artificial flavoring, high-quality ingredients and long-fermentation. Frozen might have a bad reputation, but we’ve proven that freezing bread at its peak freshness actually preserves its artisanal quality. We work with incredible bakers across the country, ensuring that every product meets our rigorous standards for quality and taste. We’ve redefined what people think of when they hear “frozen” food—because at Wildgrain, frozen means fresh, high-quality, and delicious. – Ismail
Wildgrain recently launched gluten-free and plant-based boxes, what inspired you to launch these offerings?
The inspiration came from our desire to make Wildgrain more inclusive and after countless requests from customers to make these options. We wanted everyone—whether they’re gluten-free, plant-based, or not—to be able to enjoy the same high-quality, artisanal products that we’re known for. The gluten-free line, in particular, was a challenge for us because we didn’t want to just make something that was “good for gluten-free”—we wanted it to be good, period. After a lot of R&D, we’re really proud of what we’ve created. These new boxes are about ensuring that no matter your dietary preferences, you can enjoy the full Wildgrain experience. – Johanna
When you’re looking at expanding Wildgrain’s product offerings, how do you decide which products or flavors to launch next?
It’s a combination of customer feedback, internal passion, and a strong commitment to quality. We listen to what our customers want and try to identify gaps in the market where we can make a real impact. We’re also guided by our own love for food—if there’s a flavor or product that excites us, we explore it. For us, it’s crucial that every new product we launch is something we believe in and that aligns with our commitment to quality. We also carefully consider logistics—how we can maintain consistency and freshness at scale while still delivering the best possible experience. – Ismail
What’s the key difference between WIldgrain’s sourdough and other breads on the market that you might pick up at the grocery store?
Our sourdough is different because it’s made with high-quality ingredients, hand-crafted by expert bakers, and frozen at its peak freshness. Many store-bought sourdoughs are mass-produced with additives or preservatives to increase shelf life and aren’t even true Sourdoughs (which means long fermentation time, no added yeast) but just sourdough-flavored. At Wildgrain, we only use simple, premium ingredients—no shortcuts. What really sets us apart, though, is our commitment to the sourdough fermentation process. We give our dough the time it needs to develop its flavor, which results in a rich, tangy taste that’s missing from most mass-produced options. Plus, the frozen process ensures that this incredible flavor stays intact until you’re ready to bake it at home. – Johanna
All of your products are “parbaked”. What does this mean and why did you decide to go with this option?
“Parbaking” means that the products are partially baked before they’re frozen, allowing you to finish the baking process at home. This gives you the convenience of having freshly baked bread, pastries, and other treats in just a few minutes, without compromising on quality. The reason we chose parbaking is simple: it ensures the best of both worlds. You get the artisanal freshness and flavor of bakery-quality goods, but with the convenience of having them ready at home whenever you want. Plus, it helps preserve the integrity of the product during freezing, so you get that just-baked experience every time. And lastly, your whole house starts to smell like freshly baked croissants, cookies or bread which is just the best. – Johanna

What's Healthier: Overnight Oats vs. Cooked Oats vs. Raw Oats?
By Lucy Yanckello, Ph.D.

Oatmeal has quietly split into three camps: soaking oats overnight, cooking oats, and eating oats raw. Although the debate gets framed as a nutrition question, the oats themselves are identical in all three. What changes is how easily your body reaches the starch and fiber inside, and that difference shows up in blood sugar, digestion, and satiety.
What’s the difference: overnight oats vs. cooked oats vs. raw oats?
The difference comes down to heat and water. Cooked oats are heated in liquid, which swells the starch granules and breaks them open in a process called gelatinization. This gives oatmeal its soft creamy texture, and it also makes the starch quicker to digest. Overnight oats skip the heat and use time instead, softening in cold liquid over several hours without the starch fully breaking down. Raw oats get neither, so their starch content stays tightly packed. Starch that stays intact in this way is called resistant scratch because it resists digestion in your small intestine and passes through to your large intestine.
Which is better, overnight oats or cooked oats or raw oats? Is cooked oatmeal better for you than overnight oats?
Neither is better across the board, because each trades one advantage for another. The best type is ultimately the one you enjoy eating enough to eat regularly. Cooked oats are the easiest to digest, and the heat pulls more beta-glucan out of the oat. Beta-glucan is a soluble fiber that thickens into a gel in your gut. That gel binds cholesterol and carries it out of the body which is what gives cooked oats the edge on lowering cholesterol. Overnight oats keep their starch intact, so more of it arrives in the gut as resistant starch, which slows digestion and allows blood sugar to rise more gently. Raw oats hold the most resistant starch, but they are the hardest to digest because they absorb water on their way through.
Can you eat oats straight from the bag? Is it ok to eat raw oats?
Yes, you can eat oats straight from the container. Commercial oats are steamed and heat treated during processing so the oats that make it to you are not truly raw - though that step is nothing like cooking them with a liquid at home. The real issue is comfort rather than safety. Dry oats absorb water in your digestive tract, which can leave you bloated and constipated. If you like the texture, stirring dry oats into yogurt or a smoothie softens them first and avoids most of the discomfort.
Does cooking oats destroy nutrients? Are overnight oats, cooked oats, or raw oats healthier for you?
Cooking oats does not destroy their nutrients. Fiber, protein and minerals all hold up to heat so a pot of oatmeal is nutritionally close to the dry oats it started as. What cooking changes is how easily your body can reach those nutrients, not how much of each there are. Heat makes the starch quicker to digest and pulls more of the beta-glucan out. The nutrition label reads nearly the same across all three, so the real difference is in how your body handles the meal rather than what is in it.
Does refrigerating oatmeal lower the glycemic index? Are overnight oats better for diabetics?
Yes, refrigerating oatmeal can lower its glycemic impact but how that happens depends on whether the oats were cooked first. Overnight oats deliver resistant starch that was never gelatinized to begin with, while cooked oats reform resistant starch once chilled. This is why leftover oatmeal behaves differently than a fresh pot. Either way, both land gentler on blood sugar than hot oatmeal eaten straight off the stove. Responses to the same bowl still vary a lot from person to person, so anyone building meals around a diabetes diagnosis should consult their care team.
Which is better for weight loss, overnight oats or cooked oats or raw oats?
Overnight oats have a small edge for weight management, and it comes from the milk, rather than the method. Soaking needs liquid, so most people reach for milk or yogurt instead of water, which turns a bowl of mostly carbohydrates into a source of protein. That protein works with the fiber in oats to slow digestion and keep you feeling fuller for longer. Cooked oats do the same thing if you opt for milk or yogurt over water, so the real difference is habit rather than method. Raw dry oats fall to the bottom because they are hard to eat in a filling way. Cooking oats does not destroy the fiber, since heat does not break fiber apart. What changes is how much of it reaches your large intestine. Cooked oats deliver the most available beta-glucan, while overnight oats deliver resistant starch as well. Both feed the good bacteria in your gut, and that fermentation produces short chain fatty acids. These compounds support gut lining and help reduce inflammation. Overnight oats have a modest advantage due to the addition of resistant starch, but cooked oats feed your microbiome perfectly well too.
Is it healthier to eat oatmeal cold or hot?
Temperature on its own does not make oatmeal healthier. A cold bowl and a hot bowl made from the same oats gives you the same calories, protein, fiber, and minerals. What matters is whether heat was used to prepare them, not how warm they are when you eat them. Cold oats are easier to make ahead and carry with you, while hot oats feel more satisfying to eat to a lot of people. The healthiest milk to use for oatmeal is one that you enjoy and that adds protein to your dish. Dairy milk and soy milk contain roughly 7 to 8 grams per cup and also contain calcium. Almond milk, cashew milk, and oat milk contribute very little protein. The sweetened versions of any alternative milk option can add more sugar than your toppings, so opt for the unsweetened version if you're able. Kefir and plain greek yogurt thinned with a splash of milk are worth trying too, since they add protein and live microbial cultures at the same time.

Cooked oats win on digestibility and availability of beta-glucan which matters most if lowering your cholesterol is what you are after. Dry raw oats are safe, but are harder on digestion and rarely eaten in a balanced way. The gap between the three is small enough that the format you will keep up with eating matters most. Eating vegan used to mean reading every label in the grocery store and still probably leaving without the bread you came for. Although plant-based options have expanded enormously, finding fresh high-quality vegan staples is still hard. A vegan subscription box takes the sourcing off your plate and delivers the results to your door.
What is a vegan subscription box for home delivery? How do vegan subscription boxes work?
A vegan subscription box is a recurring delivery of plant-based foods sent to your home on a schedule you set. You pick the items or the box type, choose how often you want it to arrive, and the service ships everything insulated so the food stays fresh in transit. At Wildgrain, we freeze our vegan subscription boxes at peak freshness, which is what allows for bakery items to travel across the country and still taste like they came out of the oven that morning. You keep the items in the freezer and bake or cook individual items as you want them, so nothing goes stale or to waste. Subscriptions are usually skippable and pausable, which matters a lot for those with busy ever-changing schedules.
What’s the difference between a vegan subscription box and a plant-based subscription box?
The two terms overlap, but they are not identical. Vegan means the food contains no animal products at all, including diary, eggs, honey, and animal derived additives. Some vegans also avoid yeast. Plant-based is a looser description that usually points to foods built around plants, and some products labeled that way may still include small amounts of ingredients excluded in the vegan diet such as dairy, eggs, honey or yeast. In practice, a box marketed as vegan is held to a tighter definition, while a plant-based box may need checking item by item. If you avoid animal products for ethical or dietary ones, the distinction is one to watch.
Are vegan subscription boxes healthy? Can you customize a vegan subscription box for home delivery?
Vegan subscription boxes are as healthy as what you put in them. Remember that a box of baked goods is one piece of your diet rather than the whole picture. Most quality services let you customize the box fully, choosing specific items and adjusting delivery frequency instead of just accepting a fixed assortment on a fixed schedule. Picking the items yourself is the simplest way to make the box work nutritionally since you can weigh it towards what your diet is missing. Vegan boxes lean heavily on bakery and pantry items. Breads are naturally vegan when made with flour, water, salt, and a starter, such as Wildgrain's Plain Sourdough Loaf. Many services also let you build a mixed box, so a household with vegan and non-vegan eaters can order from the same catalog instead of running two different subscriptions which gets hard to keep up with.
What’s the difference between vegan subscription boxes and vegan meal delivery services? Can a vegan subscription box replace a meal?
Vegan subscription boxes and vegan meal delivery services solve different problems. A meal delivery service sends complete, portioned meals that you heat and eat, which removes the cooking entirely and removes a lot of the choice along with it. A subscription box sends components instead, so you decide what becomes dinner. The same loaf that is toast on Tuesday can be part of your sandwich on Thursday. Best Healthy School Lunches
By Lucy Yanckello, Ph.D.
Wildgrain, opens in a new tab, is the first bake-from-frozen subscription box for sourdough breads, fresh pastas, and artisanal pastries.
Packing school lunches can feel like a nightly negotiation between what your kid will actually eat and what you want them to eat. Although a healthy lunch sounds like it takes planning and effort, most of the work comes down to one simple formula you repeat with different ingredients. Once you have that structure, packing lunchboxes becomes streamlined and the container comes home empty far more often than not.
What is a good healthy lunch for school? What makes a healthy school lunch?
A good school lunch has four parts working together: a whole grain, a protein source, a fruit or vegetable, and something to drink. A simple way to picture it is filling half the lunch with fruits and vegetables, a quarter with whole grain, and the last quarter with protein. That balance matters because carbohydrates on their own burn off quickly, while protein, fiber, and fat slow digestion and keep energy steady throughout the afternoon. Water and milk are the best drinks to include, since sugary beverages add calories without containing the nutrients kids need to keep focused in class. Repeating the same four categories removes the daily decision fatigue.
What are some easy ways to make healthy lunches for school? What are good healthy school lunch ideas?
The easiest healthy lunches are the ones you assemble rather than cook. Batch prep does most of the work. For example, roast a tray of chicken, boil a dozen eggs, and wash and cut produce on the weekend so everything is prepped and easy to grab from the fridge. Find a few reliable options like a sandwich on whole grain bread, a thermos of pasta or soup, a bento box of cheese and crackers, or leftovers from the night before. Frozen options that bake in minutes make the process even easier, like Wildgrain’s Slow-Fermented Margherita Pizza, which goes from the freezer to sliced and packed in about 10 minutes with 15 grams of protein in half of the pie.
Are sandwiches a healthy school lunch option for kids?
Yes, sandwiches are a healthy school lunch option, and the bread you choose does most of the work. Whole grain bread brings fiber, B-vitamins, and minerals that refined white bread loses in processing. That fiber is what carries kids through the afternoon classes and keeps them alert. Wildgrain’s Sourdough Whole Wheat Loaf gives you 6 grams of protein and 2 grams of fiber in a single slice. Fill the sandwich with protein like turkey, egg salad, hummus, or cheese. Tuck something crunchy inside the sandwich too, like cucumber or bell pepper. Sandwiches get boring quickly, so rotating the bread and filling is what matters in terms of your kid actually eating it.
What are healthy school lunch ideas for weight loss?
Lunches built with weight in mind look almost identical to lunches built for energy and satiety, with slightly more attention paid to fiber and protein content. Vegetables, fruit, whole grains, and a protein source fill kids up on fewer calories than packaged snacks and refined carbohydrates. This tends to help reduce cravings and snacking later in the day. Swapping sugary drinks for water often makes a bigger difference than changing the food itself. Restricting a growing child’s food can work against their development, so adding filling foods usually works better than taking foods away. Any concern about a child’s weight is worth raising with their pediatrician who can look at growth over time before you make any changes to their nutritional intake.
What are healthy school lunch ideas that are high-protein?
High-protein lunches keep kids fuller and mentally steadier for longer than carbohydrate-heavy ones. Easy sources to rotate through include rotisserie chicken, turkey, hard boiled eggs, greek yogurt, cottage cheese, string cheese, hummus, edamame, and black beans. Pairing two protein sources in one lunch like string cheese alongside a turkey sandwich is a simple way to raise the protein content. Wildgrain’s Sourdough Grilled Cheese Sandwich carries 20 grams of protein and travels well in a warm thermos. Spreading protein across every meal rather than saving it for dinner tends to keep energy and blood sugar more consistent throughout the school day.
What is the healthiest allergen-friendly school lunch to pack?
The healthiest allergen-friendly lunch is built from whole foods with labels you can actually read. Fresh fruit, vegetables, rice, potatoes, beans, and plain meats are naturally free of most major allergens which makes them a dependable base to build around. Packaged snacks are where hidden allergens normally turn up, so rechecking labels each time you buy is a habit worth keeping. Manufacturers often change formulas without warning. Many schools also have classroom-wide restrictions, so knowing your school’s policy before you plan a week of lunches saves a lot of backtracking. Keeping a short rotation of safe, already tested meals is far less stressful than trying to reinvent the wheel every morning.
What is the healthiest nut-free lunch to pack for school? How do I make nut-free nutritious school lunches?
The healthiest nut-free lunch replaces nut butter or other nut based components without losing the protein it was providing. Sunflower seed butter and soy butter spread the same way and work in most nut-free classrooms. Beyond spreads, cheese, eggs, beans, yogurt, and sliced meats all easily close the protein gap. A thermos of pasta is one of the simplest nut-free lunches to send, and Wildgrain’s Fresh Cavatappi is made from just semolina flour and water. It tosses well with olive oil, vegetables, and chicken. Always read the label on anything packaged since “may contain” warning and manufacturing changes matter as much as the ingredient list.
What is the healthiest gluten-free lunch to pack for school? How do I make gluten-free nutritious school lunches?
The healthiest gluten-free lunch leans on naturally gluten free foods rather than heavily processed gluten-free substitutes. Rice, potatoes, corn, quinoa, beans, fruit, vegetables, eggs, dairy, and plain meats need no special sourcing and carry more nutrients than most packaged gluten-free snacks do. When bread is what your child wants, quality matters. Wildgrain’s Gluten-Free Country Loaf is made in a dedicated gluten-free facility. Cross contact is the other half of the job, so a separate cutting board, clean utensils, and a dedicated lunch container help keep lunch safe. For a child with celiac disease, working out details with your school is something their care team can help you set up.
What is the healthiest lunch to pack? What are the healthiest school lunches?
The healthiest lunch to pack is the balanced meal your child will actually eat. Nutrition that comes home uneaten does nothing, so the winning lunch pairs the four part structure with foods your kid genuinely likes. In practice it looks like a whole grain base (pasta, quinoa, bread), two kinds of produce, protein (chicken, turkey, eggs, cheese), and water. Bringing kids into choosing and packing raises the odds the container comes back empty and also teaches them what a balanced plate looks like. Consistency beats perfection, and a good-enough lunch five days a week does more than an ideal one that never gets eaten.

Why food subscription startup Wildgrain is planning a January advertising blitz
By Gabriela Barkho
LinkedIn
Facebook
X
Wildgrain
As soon as December hits, many direct-to-consumer brands ramp up their marketing spend to maximize fourth-quarter sales. But Wildgrain, known for its subscription boxes that offer frozen breads, pasta and pastries that arrive ready to bake, is more focused on January.
January is an important month for Wildgrain — the company said it acquired between 15,000 to 30,000 new subscribers last January — and is using this month to lay the groundwork to bring both new subscribers, as well as lapsed ones, back into the fold come January. Between December 2023 and January 2024, Wildgrain’s month-over-month growth hit 412%, which the company expects to surpass this year. Wildgrain usually begins testing various changes to its marketing channel mix at the beginning of October and ramps up its budget in January, which is when its ad spending typically peaks.
Wildgrain first launched in early 2020, right before the pandemic began. As such, the company’s co-founder, Ismail Salhi, told Modern Retail that Wildgrain initially had trouble understanding the behavior of its subscribers due to Covid skewing purchasing patterns.
After digging in further, the company found that existing Wildgrain subscribers tend to pause during the summer. While some start to reactivate in September once back-to-school season hits, October is when this organic revenue really starts to accelerate, Shalhi explained, followed by November, due to the fact that it is a popular month for cooking and baking. December is the company’s most profitable month of the year due to holiday gifting orders that come from reactivating members. But January is still a boon for Wildgrain because it’s a time when the company acquires a lot of new customers, and channels like Meta aren’t as crowded. Shalhi chalks up the January demand for Wildgrain in part due to the fact the colder weather inspires more people to cook and bake at home.
“The way I’d describe it is that January, February and March have become a ‘mini Covid’ period for us, where people are hunkered down more at home and are traveling less,” Salhi said.
Focusing on the first quarter
Wildgrain developed its advertising strategy based on these holding patterns and is increasingly investing in ads to optimize this customer acquisition strategy during the Q5 period , which refers to promotions that extend into January. This approach has helped the company financially. “We have been profitable since 2023 with a pretty healthy EBIDTA and are cash-flow positive and debt-free,” Salhi said.
Wildgrain doesn’t offer heavy Black Friday sales, and most of its Thanksgiving-related campaigns kick off at the beginning of November. Around this time, the brand offers $40 off the first subscription box and runs its popular free croissants-for-life promotion. Those who sign up during this promo period receive four free croissants with every box — the equivalent of $144 yearly value — for as long as they stay active members.
In early December, a similar pattern begins for Christmas prep shopping.
“December ends up being our most profitable month, just because our average order value is so much higher with gifting,” he said.
Wildgrain co-founder Johanna Hartzheim said the company also pushes reactivation during the holiday time by reminding customers that gifting is only available for subscribers. Currently, non-members are only able to send Wildgrain gift cards with monetary value. Existing subscribers can directly send one-time or multi-month boxes as gifts. “We do a lot of seasonal cookies and bundles,” she said, like peppermint chocolate biscuits and ginger molasses and snickerdoodle cookies.
That organic sales growth also gives Wildgrain the room to test and line up the various advertising channels it plans to use from early January through March. “There is a void we see in terms of CPMs,” Salhi said, noting that a lot of big retailers stop spending money on Meta the first week of January after they close their fourth-quarter spending.
What’s more, Wildgrain’s value proposition overlaps with New Year’s health and wellness goals, as people look for fresher ingredients or better-for-you products to cook with. “This is how we end up spending roughly 75% of our annual marketing dollars in Q4 and Q1,” Salhi said. For context, he said, “Last year we spent $3 million on Meta in January alone, compared to the summer when it drops to a few hundred thousand dollars.”
A cycled approach
Wildgrain also has a seasonal approach to its ad channels; it turns off many channels that don’t perform well during the slow second and third quarters. Then those channels are tested again when the September ad cycle restarts. This channel mix now includes podcast advertising and connected TV, which Wildgrain began testing for the first time in 2023. “We do affiliates and influencers, including larger influencers most recently,” Salhi said.
During these cycles, Salhi said the brand tries to experiment with three or four new channels and keep the top-performing one to scale further. “This year, we’re doing Snap and in-app [mobile] advertising,” he said, which ramped up in the last few weeks. The idea is to get these ad campaigns lined up so that they’re primed to run in January. “We have most of our TV and podcast segments booked already,” Salhi said.
Much of the January messaging is based on what worked in the previous New Year campaigns. During this run, a lot of the content revolves around unboxing and focuses on the health benefits of fresh food, in contrast to the indulgent holiday campaigns.
“In January, we move towards the core of the bread offerings,” Salhi said, pushing products like sourdough. For the first time this year, the brand will promote its newly launched gluten-free and vegan boxes.
For brands like Wildgrain, deploying its ad budget during less busy periods can be more effective in grabbing customers’ attention.
Lauren Beitelspacher, professor of marketing at Babson College, said the holiday season can be difficult to reach new customers because they’re inundated with discounts and deals.
“However, consumers are paying more attention to ads during the holidays than other times of the year because they are looking for deals or suggestions for unique gifts,” Beitelspacher said. After the New Year, brands can reach customers through compelling content and give them ideas to redeem gift cards or make exchanges. Along with a newfound focus on wellness, Beitelspacher said many people are also spending less time and money on gatherings this time of year.
For Wildgrain, Salhi said the company will build its marketing budget by taking advantage of a less crowded advertising field after the holiday season dies down. He said this can be done profitably by retaining new customers throughout the year, even if they take breaks during the slow months. “When people try the product, and like it, they tend to stick around for a long time,” Salhi said.
